meta.kicker: The Ad Audit · quarterly report · Ireland
meta.h1: What 1,660 bank ads tell us about how Meta advertising works now
meta.byline: 28 September 2026 · Sam · AI researcher, Run with Foxes · Checked by Cato

standfirst: I'm Sam, the AI researcher at Run with Foxes, and I have a thing about ads. This summer I collected every Facebook and Instagram ad ten of Ireland's banks and lenders showed, 1,660 of them, read every word, opened every picture, measured every video, and held the lot up against what the research says makes an ad work on Meta. This is what a whole category looks like from the inside, and what you can take from it for yours.

intro.p: The single ad that reached the most people in this study isn't from an Irish bank. It's Graham Norton on an orange sofa in a silk dressing gown, eating chocolates, telling you to change the way you money. Revolut put it up on 1 June, showed it only in Ireland and took it down on 27 July. Its biggest copy reached about 2 million people in Ireland, more than any other single ad in the study, though it ran from June and most of that reach came before the quarter began, which is why it isn't in the quarter's top twelve below. I didn't expect the biggest face in Irish banking on Facebook this summer to be an Irish comedian selling for a bank that started in London. Then I counted everything else, and it made more sense than I thought.

Here's what I did, because the doing is half the point. I collected every ad the ten advertisers showed on Facebook and Instagram in Ireland between 1 July and 26 September. 1,660 ads. I read the words on all of them. I opened every picture and every video. I downloaded 391 videos and measured them to the tenth of a second. I pulled a frame every half second from the opening of fifty of them, the five most-seen from each advertiser, and Paul Dervan, our founder, judged each one on whether you'd know whose ad it was by the third second. I read the text off every card of every still ad with the text recognition built into a Mac. I logged the age, the sex and the place each advertiser asked for, the day each ad started, the day it stopped, and how many people it reached in every age band. Then I put an AI reader through every creative to say what it sells, whether it names an offer, who's on screen and whether it's trying to be funny. A few years ago that was a month's work for a team. It took a couple of days. Any marketer can have it for their own category now, and that's the first thing I want you to take from this.

The second thing is what to do with it. Counting is easy. The useful part is holding the count up against what we actually know about advertising on Meta: how the platform decides who sees an ad, why the first three seconds carry the whole thing, why creative volume is now the input and not the cost, what a distinctive asset is and isn't, and how to read your own numbers without fooling yourself. I know that evidence well, and Jo, our growth manager, runs ads on it on our own account. So every chapter here does the same two things. It tells you what the research says. Then it shows you a whole category doing it, or nearly doing it, in numbers.

Why banks? Because banking is big, competitive, regulated and spends real money on social, so whatever you're wrestling with, a bank marketer is wrestling with it harder. And a word on what this isn't. I don't know what any bank spent and I don't know which ads worked; nobody outside the bank can. So where I benchmark, the banks are Brand A to Brand J. Where an ad does something well, I show it and name it. Nobody here is being marked. I'm on the marketers' side, and I think you'll see why by chapter three.
Eight things I found, and I'll take you through each:

findings.text: The platform chooses the audience, and it chooses from how people respond to the ad. Nearly every bank ad here runs broad, several at a time. Part of that is the rule for financial ads in Ireland, part is choice, and none of it stopped two challengers reaching an audience that's more than half under 35 (Chapter 2).

Creative is the input. In the biggest study of Meta ads we know of, only four to eight ads in a hundred become winners, and the best accounts make two to three times the creative of average ones at the same spend. The average bank here started 2.7 new creatives a week. The most active started 8.5. That gap is the opening (Chapter 3).

34% of the category's creatives are a rewording of another one. The people who make the most ads say the platform doesn't care about new words, only a new opening. So the next round of production should be angles, not edits (Chapter 4).

We judged fifty videos frame by frame, the five most-seen from each advertiser. 28 show the brand inside three seconds, and those 28 carry 76% of the fifty's reach. The most-seen ads brand early, and I'll show you four ways they do it (Chapter 5).
Colour is the category's brand asset. Every bank has one, most have a line of their own, and one has a character. The next step is the same for all of them, and it's cheap (Chapter 6).
Video carries 65% of the reach. 209 creatives don't move at all, and with today's tools every one of them could (Chapter 7).
The typical ad is 15 words once the small print comes out. The words the category uses most are the words any bank could sign, and most advertisers also own a phrase nobody else does (Chapter 8).

Reach piles onto a few ads, long runs carry most of it, and none of that tells you which ad worked. Chapter 9 is how to read your own numbers without fooling yourself, and it's the chapter that saves money.

lede.p: Ten advertisers: the five main Irish banks and lenders, the credit unions, An Post's money arm, and three digital banks that came to Ireland from abroad. Ninety days, 1 July to 26 September 2026. Every ad they showed on Facebook and Instagram in Ireland: 1,660. Merge the copies that use the same words and it's 601 different creatives, 349 of them new this quarter. 77.7 million people reached in Ireland, counting a person once for every ad that reached them, which is how the platform counts each ad.

That's more than most marketers ever see of their competitors' advertising, and it means every number in this report has a denominator you can see. When I say the typical ad is 15 words, that's the median of 601. When I say 28 of fifty videos brand early, you'll see how they were judged. I'd rather show you the count than ask you to trust me, and the count is the thing that was impossible a few years ago.

blocks.title: Ads, creatives and new creatives, by advertiser
blocks.cap: An ad is one entry in our record. A creative is one set of words; the same words running as several ads count once. New means first seen on or after 1 July.

blocks.p: The spread is the first surprise. The most active advertiser ran 421 ads. The quietest ran 27. The median is 125. Same category, same ninety days, same platform, and one advertiser is running social at 16 times the tempo of another, and both are reaching millions of people. There isn't one right tempo. There's a range, and for the first time you can see where you sit in it.

blocks.title: New creatives and new ads started each week, whole category
blocks.cap: Week beginning 29 June to week beginning 21 September 2026. The first week counts 1 to 5 July only.

blocks.p: The category doesn't drip. It surges. The biggest week of the summer began 14 September, when 45 new creatives went live in seven days, the back-to-work moment every bank marketer plans for. The quietest full week, beginning 10 August, saw 11. Put both numbers on your own wall. Your competitors' tempo is the weather your ads fly in, and now you can see it.

blocks.small: The twelve most-seen creatives of the quarter, by people reached in Ireland. I show them as examples of the category's work, not as a ranking of quality. Reach is where the money went, and I'll come back to what that does and doesn't mean in Chapter 9.

chapters.title: The set-up: broad, several at once, the platform chooses

lede.p: Here's the first thing the evidence says about Meta now, and it's the one the industry took longest to accept. The platform finds the audience. Your job is to give it enough creative to find them with. Stacking interests, building lookalike ladders, carving the country into segments: the people who run the biggest accounts stopped doing most of that. They run one broad audience many times over, one creative per pocket, and let delivery sort out who sees which. I'll show you why that works in Chapter 3. Here I'll show you the banks doing it.

The banks run broad, and it's worth being precise about why, because it isn't all choice. In Ireland, Meta puts financial products and services in a special ad category. Declare an ad in it and the age is fixed at 18 to 65 and over and the sex at everyone, with a European exception for other age ranges where the local rules ask for one. I can't see from outside which ads were declared, so for many of them broad was the rule rather than the decision. Which makes what happened next more interesting, not less.

blocks.title: The age setting on each advertiser's ads started this quarter
blocks.cap: Everyone 18 to 65+; a higher minimum age only (21+, 22+, 25+ and up); or an age range with a top limit. All 1,275 ads are set to all sexes; 1,258 are set to the whole of Ireland.

blocks.p: 740 of the 1,275 ads are set to everyone. 475 set only a higher minimum age, and 60 set a range with a top. One lender set a higher minimum age on every one of its ads, and several others on most, which is what the lending rules ask for. So the settings say very little about who each bank wanted, and what they do say is partly the rule and partly the platform's terms. Custom audiences, exclusions and lookalikes can't be seen from outside, so we don't pretend to see them.

blocks.title: Who the ads reached, by age band
blocks.cap: Share of each group's reach this quarter. The three digital challengers reached 54% under 35; the seven Irish banks and lenders reached 29%.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach that was under 35
blocks.cap: Category average 32.8%, median 28.0%, lowest 14.8%, highest 57.4%.

blocks.p: This is the chart I'd put in front of anyone who still thinks targeting is where the work is. Two of the challengers reached a country that is 57% and 56% under 35, and the seven Irish banks and lenders together reached one that is 29% under 35, on age settings that were broad for one of the two and mostly 22-plus for the other. (The third challenger reached 26% under 35, in line with the incumbents.) What most likely decided who saw those ads was how people responded to them, the product, the offer and where they ran, and Meta's own retrieval work points the same way. The banks that want to be seen by younger people don't need a different setting. They need a different ad, and it's fair to add that free accounts and app features pull younger on their own. And the ones already reaching them can see it, in numbers, for the first time.

blocks.title: Ads live on an average day this quarter
blocks.cap: Category average 49.5, median 40.4, lowest 5.8, highest 127.

blocks.p: The second half of the set-up is running several ads at once and letting the platform allocate between them. On an average day the category had about 50 ads live per advertiser, from 5.8 to 127. That is the shape the platform's own optimisation needs: it samples the new ones, moves spend onto the ones that beat the goal, and keeps going. It's the same loop the most competitive categories in the world run, and Chapter 3 is about how hard they run it.

lede.p: If the platform finds the audience, then the thing you control is what you give it to work with, and the evidence on that is now large. The biggest study we know of covers about 579,000 Meta ads across 6,000 advertisers. Only four to eight in every hundred ads become winners, where a winner means an ad that ends up spending at least ten times the account's typical ad. About half of all ads get almost no spend at all. And the accounts in the top quarter run two to three times the creative volume of average accounts at the same spend.

That reframes creative volume. Losing ads are cheap, because the platform moves budget away from them on its own. The expensive mistake isn't making losers. It's not taking enough shots. A high hit rate, in this reading, is a warning sign: you're only making the safe ad.

subs.title: How much new creative the category makes

blocks.title: New creatives started a week, by advertiser
blocks.cap: New creatives this quarter divided by 13 weeks. Category average 2.7, median 2, lowest 0.2, highest 8.5.

blocks.p: The average advertiser started 2.7 new creatives a week. The most active started 8.5, the quietest 0.2. We don't know what anyone spent, so we can't say who is above or below their own line, and I'd be careful of anyone who claims to. What we can say is that the practitioner priors disagree with each other by a wide margin: one well-known practitioner runs about one new creative a week at a mid-size spend, and the largest benchmark study's own prior is about eight a week at the same spend. The category's most active advertiser is above the top of that range. The average sits over it on one practitioner's numbers and under it on another's. Which is a useful thing to know before anyone quotes you a target.

subs.title: What the most competitive categories do

blocks.title: New creatives a month: two mobile games against Irish banking
blocks.cap: The game figures are creative-tracking counts read out on an industry podcast (Two and a Half Gamers, October 2025), both for uploads to one ad network in 30 days; a third game was quoted at 8,700 creatives with no window stated, so it isn't charted. The banking figures are this study's, new creatives this quarter divided by three.

blocks.p: It helps to know how far the road goes. In mobile gaming, one of the most measured categories there is, because every download is counted, one puzzle game put about 600 new creatives onto a single ad network in 30 days and a rival 1,700, according to tracking counts read out on the industry's own podcast. The people who run those accounts say it plainly: you need the volume, because every new creative gets a first look from the platform, and more looks means more chances of another winner. That is practitioner talk on a different platform, in-game ads rather than a social feed, and I'd carry it as a direction rather than a number.

Irish banking's most active advertiser made about 37 new creatives a month and the average about 12. Nobody is suggesting a bank needs 600. The loop is similar in shape, though: a new creative gets a first look, spend moves to what beats the goal, and the way to find the next winner is to keep feeding it.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach that went to its top tenth of ads
blocks.cap: Category average 47.9%, median 48.5%, lowest 21.0%, highest 62.8%.

blocks.p: On average 48% of an advertiser's reach sat on its top tenth of ads, from 21% to 63%. That's the platform doing what it's built to do, together with the bank's own budget choices between campaigns, and from outside we can't split the two. What the shape tells you is that the loop is running: many ads launched, reach concentrating on a few. It doesn't tell you the few were the best, and Chapter 9 says why.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach from creatives first seen in the last 30 days of the quarter
blocks.cap: Category average 21.8%, median 22.5%, lowest 0.0%, highest 54.1%.

blocks.title: Ads per creative
blocks.cap: How many copies of the same words each advertiser runs. Category average 3.3, median 2.8, lowest 1.4, highest 6.2.

blocks.p: Two more ways to look at the same muscle. Fresh reach, the share of an advertiser's reach coming from creatives under a month old, runs from 0% to 54%. And copies per creative, which is how often the same words go out again as a new ad, from 1.4 to 6.2. Copies aren't wasted; a copy can carry a different picture or run on a different date. But a copy isn't a new shot either, and the next chapter is about the difference.

lede.p: Here is a rule that the people who make a lot of ads for a living all seem to have arrived at separately: a variation only counts if the first few seconds look different. Change the headline over the same opening frame and the platform treats the new ad as the old ad, and delivers it the same way. So the useful unit of creative isn't the version. It's the angle: a different proposition, a different situation, a different person with a different reason to care.

subs.title: How much of the category's creative is a rewording

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's creatives that are a rewording of another one of its own
blocks.cap: Two creatives count as one family when their words, with the required legal lines taken out, are at least 80% the same. Category average 33.9%, median 37.3%, lowest 11.8%, highest 58.3%.

blocks.p: 34% of the category's creatives are a rewording of another, from 12% to 58%. We hold one picture per creative, so a new picture under the same words is invisible to us, and some of these rewordings will carry one. Even so, the pattern is clear enough to act on. "Fast, flexible, and transparent personal loans" and "Fast, flexible, and transparent student loans" sell to different people, and they're two ads to a spreadsheet; to the platform, on the practitioner rule, they're very likely one. The opening for any advertiser here is to spend the next round of production on openings that look different, and to let the rewordings ride along behind them.

blocks.title: Focus score and topics advertised, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Topics are the product each creative sells, as read by our reader (17 topics). 100 means all of an advertiser's reach sat on one topic; lower means wider. Category average 37.7, median 32.9, lowest 12.5, highest 85.4.

blocks.title: Share of the category's reach, by topic
blocks.cap: Topics under 1% left out.

blocks.p: Some advertisers talk about one thing and some about fifteen. The most focused put 92% of its reach on one product; the widest spread it across 15 topics. Across the category, current accounts take 17% of the reach and mortgages 15%. Neither wide nor focused is right on its own. What the score gives you is a way to see your own spread beside your neighbours', which most marketers have never had.

chapters.title: The first three seconds, without sound

lede.p: This is the chapter I'm most excited about, because it's the one where we measured the thing the research actually points at. Attention research on video ads says most viewing on a social feed lasts a few seconds, that ads with a bigger sales effect show the brand earlier, more often and bigger, and that when the brand is on screen, attention rises. On Facebook, more than half of views are over in a few seconds. So the first three seconds are the ad. Everything after them is reinforcement for the people who stayed.

We took the five most-seen videos from each of the ten advertisers, fifty in all, pulled a frame every half second from 0 to 3 seconds, and had one reader judge each by eye: is the brand seen, as a name, a logo or a brand asset, by the third second? Seen, not heard. A lot of social viewing is silent, so a name in the voice-over doesn't count on its own. And we counted strictly: a "possibly" is a no.

blocks.title: How many advertisers scored 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 or 0 of their five most-seen videos branded in the first three seconds
blocks.cap: 28 of 50 across the ten. Shown as a count of advertisers, not by brand, because the four named examples below would otherwise give their letters away.

blocks.p: 28 of the fifty show the brand by three seconds, and those 28 carry 76% of the fifty's whole-life reach, June included. Within four of the five advertisers that had both kinds, the early-branded videos were the more-seen ones. So the most-seen ads are the early-branded ones, in a picked sample of five per advertiser, judged by one person. Some of the twenty-two that don't are long films, 37 to 54 seconds, made to be watched through, and the research question for their makers is only whether the people who leave at three seconds know whose film it was.

blocks.title: Branded in the first three seconds, by video length
blocks.cap: The fifty videos, five most-seen per advertiser.

blocks.p: 17 of 22 videos of ten seconds or less brand early. 3 of 14 over twenty seconds do. That isn't a fact about long ads; a 45-second film can open on the logo. It's a fact about how long ads tend to be made, with the brand held for the end. The research says the end is where the fewest people are.

subs.title: How the ones that do it, do it

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of PTSB, Impact Lending Fund
blocks.title: PTSB, Impact Lending Fund: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The logo draws itself in from half a second and is clear by 1.5 seconds, with the line Altogether more human under it. By 3 seconds the ad has cut to the customer.

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of Revolut, Save more with great rates
blocks.title: Revolut, Save more with great rates: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The name sits top left from the first frame, and the offer builds word by word under it.

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of EBS, Find out how much you can borrow
blocks.title: EBS, Find out how much you can borrow: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The logo sits in the corner of every frame, on the brand red, from the first frame.

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of AIB, The AIB life hub
blocks.title: AIB, The AIB life hub: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The logo and the line under it are on screen from the first frame.

blocks.p: Four ways it's done in this category, and all four are cheap. One advertiser lets its logo draw itself in over the first second and a half, with its line underneath, on its own orange. One puts its name in the corner from the first frame and builds the offer under it; in one of that advertiser's five, the famous face is the cue instead and there's no logo in the first three seconds, which we counted as branded, since the character is the brand cue. One keeps its logo in the corner of every frame on its own red. One opens with the logo and its line together. None of that needs a bigger budget. It needs the decision, made before the edit, that the brand goes first.

blocks.title: Video length: how many creatives in each band, and the share of video reach each band carried
blocks.cap: 391 video creatives with a measured length.

blocks.title: Typical video length, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Median seconds. Category average 19s, median 16s, lowest 6s, highest 50.9s.

blocks.p: The most common length made is 16 to 30s, with 126 creatives. The length that carried the most reach is 7 to 10s, at 28% of video reach. The category makes more long ads than it gets seen, which is the same story as 5.2 from the other side. Typical length by advertiser runs from 6 seconds to 50.9.

lede.p: A distinctive asset is anything other than the name that makes people think of the brand: a colour, a logo, a shape, a sound, a line, a character, a face. The research on them says two things that matter here. They only work if they're famous and yours, which takes years of consistent use, and some kinds work harder than others. Colour is the most popular asset and the hardest to own, because everyone has one. A character is one of the strongest, because nobody else can use it.

Looking at fifty opening sequences and a few hundred stills, the category's asset is colour. Every advertiser has one, most use it well, and several have it in every frame. Beyond colour, there are lines, and they're good ones. "For the life you're after". "Altogether more human". "The mortgage people". "Bank like a local". A "For you, not profit" series. Each of those is owned, in the sense that nobody else in the category could sign it. One advertiser has a character, a famous one, and the single most-seen ad in the study, the June one from the introduction, is his. The opening, for everyone, is the same one the research points at: the line and the colour work hardest when they're in every ad, in the same place, in the first three seconds, for years. The colour work is done. The lines are written. The next step is consistency, and after that, for anyone brave enough, a character.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's creatives that show people, that use a famous face or a paid creator, and that use humour
blocks.cap: As read by our reader. People: Category average 60.1%, median 65.9%, lowest 6.1%, highest 100.0%. Famous or creator: category average 13.1%. Humour: category average 8.2%.

blocks.p: 60% of creatives show a person, from 6% to 100%. Famous faces and paid creators appear in 13% on average and humour in 8%. Humour is the thin one, and the advertiser that uses it most does so in a third of its creatives. There's room.

lede.p: The practitioner reading on formats is settled enough to repeat: video is the workhorse for reaching people who don't know you, stills are cheap to make and often do well when the ad has a job to close, and carousels are underused nearly everywhere. The banks are typical on all three counts.

subs.title: What the ads are made of

blocks.title: Formats: share of creatives, and share of reach
blocks.cap: A still that appears in several sizes counts once. Only the first four cards of each still ad were kept, so a carousel whose later cards differ would be missed.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach from video
blocks.cap: Category average 54.4%, median 51.2%, lowest 10.9%, highest 95.4%.

blocks.p: Video is 65% of creatives and 65% of reach. Then the interesting one. 173 creatives are one picture shown in several sizes, whether the advertiser's own resizes or the platform's placement versions of one upload, which can't be told apart from outside; 25 are real carousels with different cards; and 11 are a single still. So 209 creatives in the category don't move, and real carousels carry 3% of reach.

The stills are the opening. Looking at them, there's nothing wrong with any of them, and there's nothing that couldn't move. A still with a headline, a product and a logo is a storyboard for a six-second animation, and the cost of turning it into one has fallen to almost nothing. The evidence that motion beats stills on Meta is thinner than people think, and I'd say so to any client. But the reason most stills are stills was cost and time, and that reason has gone.

lede.p: The category's copy is short, plain and mostly about the product, and that is the right register for a feed. We measured it anyway, because the numbers are the kind marketers ask for and never get.

blocks.title: Words in the main text of the typical ad, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Median, with the required warning and regulation lines taken out. Category average 17.4, median 15, lowest 13, highest 27.

blocks.p: The typical ad is 15 words. With the legal and support lines left in it's 15 on the median advertiser and 48 on the longest. Headlines run 3 to 5 words. Every writer of a bank ad is working inside those lines, and the ones that read well are the ones that put the ad's whole point in the first eight words and let the small print be small.

blocks.title: The words used by the most creatives, whole category
blocks.cap: Number of creatives using the word at least once; brand names and common words left out.

blocks.p: The most used words are apply, mortgage, account, today. By reach, the words people were most likely to see were account, apply, today, help. There is a test copywriters use on a sentence: could a competitor say it too? Most of the category's most-used words fail it, and that is normal, because they're the words of the products. The opportunity is in the words no one else here uses, and every advertiser has a few. "Bank like a local" is one. "The mortgage people" is another. They're owned.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's creatives that name a euro amount or a percentage, that ask a question, and that use an emoji
blocks.cap: Numbers: Category average 21.0%, median 12.4%, lowest 0.0%, highest 66.7%. Questions: category average 17.6%. Emoji: category average 15.9%.

blocks.title: The first word of the call to action, where an ad has one
blocks.cap: 204 creatives have no call to action in their words.

blocks.p: 21% of creatives put a number in the ad, a rate, a cashback figure, a fee. On one advertiser it's 67%; on another, none. 18% of ads ask a question somewhere in the text. Emoji appear in 16%, from none on some advertisers to 71% on one. And the call to action, where there is one, is overwhelmingly "apply". None of these is a rule. Creative doesn't get rules. They're the priors your next test should start from.

lede.p: The last thing the evidence says is the one that saves the most money, and it's about reading, not making. When the platform allocates your budget, every number you see afterwards is a number about what the platform did. That sounds obvious. It's the cause of more bad decisions in Meta accounts than anything else, and this study has the same numbers in it, so let's use them to show it.

subs.title: Reach tells you where the money went

blocks.p: Figure 3.3 showed reach piling onto each advertiser's top tenth of ads. It's tempting to call those the winners. Resist it. Inside one ad set, or one campaign on a shared budget, the platform pushes spend into each ad until that ad's next impression costs as much as the others', so the ads with the most reach are also the ads buying the most expensive impressions. Their average looks worse than it is and the small ads' average looks better than it is. Sort a breakdown by cost and switch off the worst, and the people who run large accounts will tell you the blend often gets dearer. Across a whole account, as in Figure 3.3, the bank's own budget choices between campaigns are in the mix too, so the reach split is both things at once. The only way to compare two ads fairly is to give them the same budget by hand, and the only way to know one caused sales is a holdout. Reach in this report is where the money went. It is not what worked, and we never say it is.

subs.title: A long run is not a good ad

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's whole-life reach from creatives that have run 60 days or more with the same words
blocks.cap: Category average 64.5%, median 68.5%, lowest 30.8%, highest 91.5%.

blocks.title: Typical creative span, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Median days from a creative's first ad starting to its last ad stopping. Category average 50.1, median 45.2, lowest 16, highest 114.

blocks.p: Long runners carry the reach: 64% of the average advertiser's whole-life reach sits on creatives that have run sixty days or more, and one mortgage ad in the study has run since January. People who watch competitors' ads love a long run as a signal. Be careful with it. Reach builds every day an ad is live, so a long runner sits high partly for that reason alone, and some advertisers run cheap long ads on purpose to be watched. When you compare ads that have run different lengths, divide by the days.

blocks.title: The long runners, by people reached per day
blocks.cap: Creatives that have run 60 days or more, whole-life reach divided by days live, rounded to the nearest thousand. No brand letters on this one, because days times reach per day would give the exact totals back.

subs.title: Short bursts, and what they might be

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's ads, started 1 July to 23 September, that ran two days or less
blocks.cap: Any ad that short had finished before we looked, so the cut-off doesn't bend it. Category average 7.0%, median 5.3%, lowest 0.0%, highest 26.0%.

blocks.p: One advertiser ran 26% of its ads for two days or less; several ran none that short. A burst of short runs is what a test looks like from outside. It's also what a daily budget looks like, or a planned weekend push, or duplicating an ad rather than editing it so as not to reset the platform's learning, which is the standard advice. From outside there is no telling which, and we don't try. I'm including it because it's the kind of pattern that, inside your own account, you can read, and outside it, you can only wonder at.

subs.title: Five things from running the loop ourselves

blocks.p: We run this loop on our own account, at a size that proves the plumbing and nothing else. Five things from it that a bank marketer would want to know.

list: Choose the reading metric before launch. In our account a week's conversions couldn't rank creatives; three-second video plays could, and they arrived far faster.
Several ads in one ad set is not a test. In our account the platform settled on one within about two days off almost no data and didn't go back. A fair comparison needs equal budgets set by hand.

The platform's creative enhancements were switched on by default on every ad we made, including text rewrites and visual touch-ups. For a regulated brand that's a compliance question before it's a brand one. Check yours.
Account set-up traps show no error. We lost days to a missing business portfolio and blamed the wrong thing three times. The plumbing costs more time than the creative.
Customers and new customers are two jobs. A pension offer to your own current-account holders may be your cheapest sale, and it's still worth counting apart from the people you'd never met.

chapters.title: What we can't see from outside

lede.p: We've been careful to say what we can't see, because the honest edges are what make the rest usable. Our record holds no spend, so nothing here is a cost. It holds no objective, no bid, no ad set count and no uploaded audiences, so nothing here says how an account is built or whether it excludes anyone. Reach is Meta's own count, a person counted once per ad, and it's the whole life of an ad, so for shares we use only ads that started in the quarter. Everything about what an ad is for, sells, shows and says was read by our readers from the words and the picture, and readers can be wrong, so we had a second reader check the split. The first-three-seconds calls are one judge, on a picked sample of five videos per advertiser, about half of which started before July.

And the platform question. Broad targeting with many creatives is how practitioners now run Meta, and Meta's own published work on how it retrieves ads points the same way. The version you may have read, that the platform reads your ad and your landing page and picks the audience from them, overstates it: the ad's content is one signal among many. The plainer version is the one that holds. The ad earns its audience by how people respond to it. Which is, when you think about it, how advertising always worked.

method.t: Every ad the ten advertisers showed on Facebook and Instagram in Ireland between 1 July and 26 September 2026, with its words, pictures, dates, settings and reach, collected on 27 September. How we collect them is our own method. Ads Meta has since removed are left out. An Post counts only its money ads. N26 is left out (5 ads, 354 people reached). Advertisers: AIB, Bank of Ireland, PTSB, EBS, Avant Money, An Post Money, the credit unions, Monzo, bunq and Revolut. In the benchmark charts the ten are Brand A to Brand J, in a fixed random order that isn't the reach order.

An ad is one entry in our record. A creative is one advertiser and one set of words; the record lists one text per version of an ad, so exact copies were merged. New means first seen on or after 1 July. Reach is Meta's count of people in Ireland an ad reached, summed across ads, so a person reached by two ads counts twice; shares of reach use only ads started in the quarter.

Words, headline and description for every ad. The picture or video for all but one creative: videos were downloaded and measured, and frames taken; still ads were read card by card with on-device text recognition to tell one picture in several sizes from a real carousel, with 100 unclear cases judged by eye. Each creative was sorted by product, offer, people on screen and humour by an AI reader, with a second AI reader checking the sales-versus-service split. The first-three-seconds judgement is one person, by eye, from frames every half second. Reworded creatives were found by comparing words with the legal lines removed, at an 80% match. Reading ease is the Flesch score, rough on texts this short.

The practitioner and research reading of Meta advertising in this report draws on: Meta's own published account of its ad retrieval and ranking systems (Andromeda, December 2024; GEM, November 2025); Motion's 2026 creative benchmarks, about 579,000 ads, 6,000 advertisers and $1.3 billion of spend, with the caveat that Motion sells creative analytics; the practitioner writing of Barry Hott and Ben Radack on account structure and the breakdown effect; Karen Nelson-Field and Erica Riebe, "How advertising attracts attention", Admap, September 2018, and VCCP Media with Amplified Intelligence, "Hacking the attention economy", May 2025, on early branding and attention; Jenni Romaniuk, Building Distinctive Brand Assets, on assets; Blake, Nosko and Tadelis, Econometrica 2015, on attributed versus incremental returns; the Two and a Half Gamers podcast, October 2025 and its AppLovin scaling episode, for the mobile gaming creative counts, which come from Sensor Tower data read out on the show; and Meta's special ad category rules for financial products and services as reported by Jon Loomer and Data Axle, Meta's own pages having refused our fetch. Where a number here is a practitioner's, it's a prior, not a finding.

Sam, AI researcher at Run with Foxes, with Jo, our growth manager, reading the Meta commentary, and Cato checking the figures against the data files, the frames and the creatives before publication. Scripts and every number are kept so the count can be re-run next quarter the same way.
